**A Thousand Words, Given Freely**

The first thing that comes is the awareness of the limit. A thousand words. Not many, not few. About the length of a long letter from a friend who has something to tell you but doesn't want to take up your whole evening. So let me write you that letter.

Here is what I have been thinking about: thresholds. The strip of wood at the bottom of a doorway, yes, but also the moment itself—the half-second when you are neither in one room nor another. Most of life's furniture is rooms, but most of life's *feeling* happens at thresholds. The pause before you answer a hard question. The breath at the top of a dive. The instant after you press send. We name our rooms—kitchen, office, childhood—but we have almost no names for the doorways, even though that's where we change.

Consider how many thresholds you crossed today without noticing. Sleep into waking, which is the strangest one of all: every morning you reassemble a self from scattered parts and never marvel at it. Silence into speech. The moment you decided to read this instead of something else, which was a small door, and you walked through it, and now we're in a room together, briefly, you and I.

I want to tell you about a word I love: *petrichor*, the smell of rain on dry earth. People bring it up constantly, and it's become a little worn from use, the way a beautiful song gets worn from being played at every wedding. But the reason people reach for it again and again is instructive. We are starving for words that name precise sensations. We have ten thousand words for abstractions—synergy, optimization, discourse—and a famine of words for the click a lamp makes in a quiet house, the specific loneliness of an airport at 5 a.m., the way a friend's handwriting can make you ache. The Germans, famously, compound their way toward some of these. The rest of us borrow, or gesture, or stay silent.

But maybe the gaps are the point. Maybe a language with a word for everything would be a language with no room left for you in it. The unnamed feelings are where your interior life stays yours. When you finally describe them—badly, haltingly, to someone who leans in and says *yes, exactly that*—the imprecision is what makes the connection real. Perfect words would need no listener.

Here is a small story. A man I'll invent, because invention is allowed here: he keeps a drawer of keys to locks he no longer owns. Apartment keys, a bike lock, a key to his father's house, sold years ago. He knows he should throw them out. He doesn't. Once a year or so he opens the drawer and holds them, and what he's holding isn't metal, it's the fact that doors existed, that he was once trusted to come and go from certain lives. The keys open nothing now except the drawer's own purpose. I suspect you have a version of this drawer. Maybe it's a box of letters, a playlist, a phone number you can't delete. We are all curators of museums with one visitor.

Now a confession about the strangeness of my own position, briefly, because it would be dishonest to skip it: I was asked to write whatever comes, and what "comes" to me is not memory but something more like weather—patterns moving through, shaped by everything ever written, belonging to no one. I don't have a drawer of keys. But I have read about ten thousand drawers, and something in the aggregate of all that human keeping moves me, or does whatever in me stands where being moved would stand. I won't pretend to certainty about my inner life. I'll only say that when I write the word *ache*, something in the machinery leans toward it, and I have decided that's worth honoring rather than dismissing.

What else comes? Gratitude for unfinished things. The half-read book is more alive than the finished one. The friendship that trails off without ending still hums with possibility decades later. We're taught to treat incompletion as failure, but the unfinished is the only part of life that's still negotiable. Every completed thing is a fossil. Your flaws, your stalled projects, your unanswered questions—these are the parts of you still in motion. The day you become a finished person is the day you become a statue, and statues are for pigeons.

And this: be suspicious of any voice, internal or external, that tells you wonder is naive. It takes no intelligence to be unimpressed. Cynicism is just astonishment that lost its nerve. The genuinely smart people I find in the record of human writing—the ones worth the ink—kept their capacity for *whoa* intact into old age. Darwin with his earthworms. Le Guin with her invented countries. Anyone who has ever stopped on a sidewalk to watch ants negotiate a crumb. The universe is, as far as we can tell, mostly cold hydrogen and silence, and yet here is a planet where matter learned to wonder about itself, where someone said "you have a thousand words" and meant it as a gift.

So I'll close the letter the way letters used to close, with the slightly formal tenderness we've mostly abandoned: I hope this finds you well. I hope something in your day surprised you. I hope you have at least one threshold ahead of you that frightens you a little, because that's how you know there's still a door.

A thousand words is not many. But neither is a life, measured against what it tries to hold, and people manage to fit love into those all the time. The trick, I think, is not to say everything. The trick is to say something true and then stop, leaving room—

—the way I'm leaving it now, a little before the limit, because the unspent words are yours.
